passages.t: Tola and Jair, the quiet years
passages.happening:
After Abimelech, a man of the tribe of Issachar named Tola ‘rose up to save Israel’. He lives at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim, judges Israel twenty-three years, dies and is buried there (verses 1-2).

After him comes Jair, from Gilead, who judges Israel twenty-two years (verse 3). “He had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys. And they had thirty towns in the land of Gilead, which to this day are called Havvoth-jair” (verse 4). When Jair dies, he is buried in Kamon (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
After the bloodshed of Abimelech's reign, the book pauses for two short notices. Each follows the same plain pattern: a name, a home, the years he judged, his death and his burial. These are sometimes called the minor judges. They are remembered not for battles but for families, wealth and quiet years.

Tola ‘rose up to save Israel’, though the text names no enemy. Perhaps the saving was the steadying of a people after a civil war. The text does not say more.

Thirty sons riding thirty donkeys was a picture of wealth and standing. Before horses became common for rulers, leaders and their families rode donkeys, as the Song of Deborah shows. Thirty sons and thirty towns suggest something close to a local ruling family.

The thirty towns are called Havvoth-jair, the tent villages of Jair. The books of Numbers and Deuteronomy credit towns of that name to an earlier Jair of the tribe of Manasseh. Some think this judge was a descendant who inherited or restored the name. Others think the two traditions describe the same settlements from different times.
passages.later: The earlier Jair appears in the time of Moses: “Jair, a descendant of Manasseh, went and captured their villages and called them Havvoth-jair” (Numbers 32:41).
passages.asks: Tola and Jair are remembered for forty-five quiet years, not for great deeds. Ask whether you value the people who keep things steady as much as the people who make headlines. And ask what kind of quiet faithfulness God might be asking of you in a season with no battle in it.

passages.t: Every god around, and two enemies
passages.happening:
“And again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD. They served the Baals, the Ashtoreths, the gods of Aram, Sidon, and Moab, and the gods of the Ammonites and Philistines. Thus they forsook the LORD and did not serve Him” (verse 6).

So the LORD's anger burns, and he sells them into the hands of the Philistines and the Ammonites (verse 7). That same year the Ammonites begin to crush the Israelites in Gilead, east of the Jordan, and they keep at it for eighteen years (verse 8). They even cross the Jordan to fight Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim, ‘and Israel was in deep distress’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The list of gods in verse 6 covers the whole region: the Baals and Ashtoreths of Canaan, the gods of Aram to the north, of Sidon on the coast, of Moab and Ammon to the east, and of the Philistines in the southwest. Elsewhere the Old Testament names some of them: Chemosh of Moab, Milcom of Ammon, and Dagon of the Philistines, who will appear in the story of Samson.

In the ancient world it was normal to honor the gods of powerful neighbors, especially when their peoples seemed to prosper. It felt like good sense, a way of covering every possibility. But Israel's covenant asked for a loyalty that belonged to the LORD alone, so this kind of hedging was a betrayal.

Two enemies are named in one breath. The Ammonites, east of the Jordan, will lead to the story of Jephthah in chapters 11 and 12. The Philistines, on the southern coast, will fill the story of Samson in chapters 13 to 16. The two oppressions may have overlapped, one from the east and one from the west. This chapter is the hinge between the two halves of the middle of the book.

The Ammonites lived east of the Jordan, north of Moab, with their capital at Rabbah, the site of the city of Amman in Jordan today.
passages.later:
Solomon later fell into the same worship of the neighbors' gods: “Solomon followed Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians and Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites” (1 Kings 11:5).

Joshua had put the choice before the people plainly, and named some of the same gods: “choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you are living” (Joshua 24:15).
passages.asks: Israel served every god around, just to be safe. Ask where you spread your trust around, a little here and a little there, so that you will never have to depend on God alone. And ask what you would lose if you put all your weight on him.

passages.t: ‘Go and cry out to the gods you have chosen’
passages.happening:
The Israelites cry out to the LORD: “We have sinned against You, for we have indeed forsaken our God and served the Baals” (verse 10).

The LORD reminds them how often he saved them: from the Egyptians, the Amorites, the Ammonites, the Philistines, the Sidonians, the Amalekites and the Maonites (verses 11-12). “But you have forsaken Me and served other gods, so I will no longer save you. Go and cry out to the gods you have chosen. Let them save you in your time of trouble” (verses 13-14).

“We have sinned,” the Israelites said to the LORD. “Deal with us as You see fit; but please deliver us today!” (verse 15).

“So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD, and He could no longer bear the misery of Israel” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
This is the book's most revealing conversation between Israel and God. For the first time the people say plainly, ‘We have sinned’. And for the first time God answers with a refusal.

The lists are each seven long, the gods Israel served and the enemies God saved them from. Seven was a number of completeness. Israel had served every god around, and God had saved them from every enemy around.

God's answer is bitter and true. ‘Go and cry out to the gods you have chosen’. The word ‘chosen’ recalls Joshua's challenge at Shechem to choose whom they would serve. Israel had chosen. Now its choice comes back to face it.

Then the people do more than speak. They hand themselves over, ‘Deal with us as You see fit’, and they put away their foreign gods.

The last words of verse 16 are among the most tender in the Old Testament. In Hebrew they say that God's soul grew short over Israel's misery, a way of saying that he could not bear it any longer. It was his patience with their suffering that ran out, not his patience with them.

The chapter does not say that God sent a deliverer next. It says only that he could not bear their misery. The next verses show the people looking for a leader on their own.
passages.later: The prophets heard the same note in God's voice. Jeremiah: “But where are the gods you made for yourselves? Let them rise up in your time of trouble and save you if they can” (Jeremiah 2:28). Hosea: “How could I give you up, O Ephraim? How could I surrender you, O Israel?” (Hosea 11:8). And Isaiah, of Israel's past: “In all their distress, He too was afflicted” (Isaiah 63:9).
passages.hard:
Did God change his mind? And was Israel's repentance real, or only a way to get relief?

God says he will no longer save them (verse 13), and then he acts for them (verse 16). Readers explain this in more than one way. Some see God's refusal as a real warning, withdrawn when Israel moved from words to action by putting away its gods. Others see it as a test of whether their repentance was sincere. Still others notice what verse 16 actually says. It does not say God was persuaded by their repentance. It says he could not bear their misery. On this reading God's compassion, not Israel's performance, moved him.

On whether the repentance was real, readers differ too. Israel did put away its foreign gods, yet the chapters that follow show little lasting change.

The text holds God's judgment and his compassion together, and it roots his mercy in his own character, not in anything Israel deserved.
passages.asks: God told Israel to go and cry to the gods they had chosen. Ask what you rely on in a crisis, and whether it could save you if you cried out to it. Israel said, ‘Deal with us as You see fit; but please deliver us today’. Ask what honest repentance looks like when the trouble you are in is of your own making. And ask how it changes your picture of God that he could not bear Israel's misery.

passages.happening:
The Ammonites gather for war and camp in Gilead. The Israelites gather and camp at Mizpah (verse 17).

The leaders of Gilead say to one another, “Whoever will launch the attack against the Ammonites will be the head of all who live in Gilead” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Mizpah means watchtower, and it was a common place name. This Mizpah was in Gilead, east of the Jordan, and it will be Jephthah's home.

The chapter ends with a question in the air: who will lead? In the earlier stories God raised up a deliverer. This time the elders go looking for one themselves, and they offer a reward, the headship of Gilead, to whoever will fight. The next chapter shows whom they found, and what that offer of power would do.
passages.later: Gilead was the land east of the Jordan given to the tribes of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh in the time of Moses and Joshua (Joshua 22:9). It will be the setting of Jephthah's whole story.
passages.asks: Gilead's leaders went looking for someone strong enough to fight and offered him power in return. Ask what you look for in a leader, and whether it is what God looks for. And ask whether you have ever been offered position in return for doing something hard, and what it did to your reasons.
